english: I close the window before sleeping.
tip: sebelum (before) takes a verb directly: sebelum tidur = before sleeping.

english: I listen to music while cooking.
tip: sambil = while (one person, two actions): makan sambil membaca = eat while reading.

english: After work I go straight home.
tip: pulang packs 'go home' into one word – langsung pulang = head straight home. There is no separate word for 'home' in the sentence.

target: Ibu membangunkan adik jam enam pagi.
english: Mom wakes my younger sibling at six in the morning.
tip: -kan makes a verb act on someone: bangun (wake up) → membangunkan (wake someone up).

target: Dia membacakan cerita untuk anaknya setiap malam.
english: She reads her child a story every night.
tip: -kan can mean doing it for someone: membaca (read) → membacakan (read aloud to someone).

english: I have bread and eggs for breakfast.
tip: sarapan is a verb all by itself – Saya sarapan roti is literally 'I breakfast bread'. No word for 'have' or 'eat' needed.

target: Saya mau pesan nasi goreng satu.
english: I want to order one fried rice.
tip: When ordering, the number usually follows the dish: nasi goreng satu – literally 'fried rice, one'.

target: Makanan di warung ini enak sekali.
english: The food at this food stall is very tasty.
tip: Sekali means very but comes after the adjective: enak sekali = very tasty, literally 'tasty very'.

english: May I have plain water?
tip: Boleh minta ...? politely asks for something: Boleh minta air? = May I have water?

english: It tastes sweet and a little spicy.
tip: -nya can mean the/its: rasa (taste) → rasanya (the taste of it).

english: The waiter brings our order.
tip: Kami means we/our but excludes the person you're talking to: pesanan kami = our order, not yours. Kita would include them.

english: The food has arrived, please eat.
tip: silakan politely invites someone to act: silakan makan = please eat.

english: Is there a bigger size?
tip: yang turns a description into the one that: yang lebih besar = the bigger one.

english: That shop is closed on Sundays.
tip: Itu comes after its noun: toko itu = that shop, literally 'shop that'. Ini (this) follows its noun the same way.

english: Prices at the market can be bargained.
tip: di- makes a verb passive: tawar (bargain) → ditawar (be bargained over).

target: Saya coba dulu baju ini, ya?
english: Let me try this shirt first, okay?
tip: dulu after a verb means first: coba dulu = try it first.

english: My order has not come yet.
tip: Belum means not yet: pesanan saya belum datang. Use belum, not tidak, for anything that could still happen.

target: Kopi di sini lebih murah daripada di hotel.
english: Coffee here is cheaper than at the hotel.
tip: lebih ... daripada compares: lebih murah daripada di hotel = cheaper than at the hotel.

target: Saya punya dua kakak dan satu adik.
english: I have two older siblings and one younger sibling.
tip: Indonesian sorts siblings by age, not gender: kakak = older sibling, adik = younger. Dua kakak never tells you brother or sister.

target: Ibu saya suka memasak di rumah.
english: My mother likes to cook at home.
tip: Possessor comes AFTER the noun: ibu saya = my mother (lit. mother I).

english: My husband likes black coffee.
tip: Adjectives follow their noun: kopi hitam is literally 'coffee black'. Noun first, adjective second – the reverse of English.

english: Our family lives in Jakarta.
tip: kami = we (not you); kita = we (with you): keluarga kami = our family.

english: His mother is sleeping in the bedroom.
tip: -nya on a noun = his/her: ibunya = his/her mother.

english: His house is big and clean.
tip: No word for 'is' before adjectives: Rumahnya besar = His house (is) big.

english: Has your younger sibling eaten yet?
tip: sudah ... belum? = already or not yet: Sudah makan belum? = Eaten yet?

english: That boy is my son.
tip: itu (that) comes after its noun: anak laki-laki itu = literally 'child male that'. ini (this) works the same way.

target: Ibu saya lebih muda dari ayah saya.
english: My mother is younger than my father.
tip: Comparisons borrow dari (from) for 'than': lebih muda dari ayah saya = more young from my father.

english: My older sibling got married last year.
tip: Verbs never change for past time: menikah stays the same. Tahun lalu (last year) alone signals it already happened.

target: Anak-anak sedang bermain di depan rumah.
english: The children are playing in front of the house.
tip: Doubling a noun makes it plural: anak-anak = children.

english: How old are you now?
tip: Berapa (how much) asks age: Berapa umur kamu = literally 'how-much age you'. No verb, no word order flip.
